source.title: Looped Diffusion Language Models
source.authors: Sang-Hun Lee; Chunsan Hong; Seungryong Kim; Jonghyun Lee; Jongho Park; Dongmin Park

record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether architecture choices at fixed parameter count have only small effects on language-model loss, using loop-design ablations rather than the scaling-law measurements in the original sources.
record.gate_note: The paper reports held-out NLL results for loop-count sweeps and loop-design ablations. These bear on V4, but it does not fit power laws in parameters, training tokens, or compute. It also reports downstream accuracy as loop count varies; those results are recorded as findings about inference-time looping, not as evidence about the stated parameter/token/pretraining-compute scaling relation.
record.test_reason: The study measures held-out language-model loss while changing shared effective depth and loop architecture at fixed parameter count, bearing on V4 in masked diffusion models. It does not fit or extrapolate scaling laws. Matched training FLOPs entail different token exposure, and inference loop sweeps also change evaluation compute.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that selective early-middle-layer looping improves masked diffusion model performance and training efficiency without adding parameters, that benefits depend on loop design, and that reasoning gains exceed those of deeper compute-comparable baselines.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares looped and non-looped masked diffusion models and ablates loop design; it does not fit scaling laws or test parameter/token scaling.
record.method_sensitivity: NLL varies with loop position, number of looped layers, and maximum loop count. The paper reports best results for early-middle layers and moderate loop counts.

fits_no_version.finding: Average downstream accuracy is 40.0% for MDM and 39.4%, 40.7%, and 41.4% for LoopMDM at S=1, 6, and 12.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Additional inference-time looping improves aggregate downstream accuracy in this tested setup; no downstream scaling prediction is fitted or validated.

record.problems: The reported architecture ablation is a single 170M-parameter LM1B setup trained for 0.1M steps; Table 4 gives no uncertainty estimates. Several test-NLL comparisons in Figure 2 are available only as plots.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1 generative perplexity, Table 2 zero-shot perplexity, and task-by-task Table 3 accuracies are not extracted because they do not measure V4's held-out pretraining-loss response to architecture. Other experiments on reasoning, Sudoku, attention, and adaptive inference do not test the listed scaling-law versions.

untested.parts: Power-law loss dependence on parameters, tokens, or training compute over orders of magnitude.
Extrapolation from small-run power-law fits to much larger runs.
Width sweeps, ordinary unshared depth sweeps at fixed parameter count, broad architecture families, and larger model scales.
Power-law forms outside text pretraining; using diffusion training alone does not test the power-law form.
Prediction of downstream performance from pretraining scale or loss.
Dependence of fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits on setup or fitting choices, and departures from fitted power laws.

missing.what: Record the same-final-NLL training-compute advantages explicitly: 3.34× on LM1B, 2.95× on OpenWebText, and 2.34× on FineWeb-Edu. These quantify architectural efficiency at fixed parameter count but do not quantify a fixed-compute loss gap.

The alternative input-injection experiment reports worse NLL than the standard MDM baseline. Its numerical magnitude is unavailable in the supplied figure text, so it cannot independently establish that architecture changes loss substantially.

record.verdict_notes: No power-law exponent or scaling-law prediction is tested. Table 4 provides no uncertainty estimates or numerical definition of 'slightly'; its modest absolute NLL differences should not be turned into categorical challenges merely because some configurations underperform baseline. The layer-count qualification also includes changing token exposure under matched training compute.

versions.untested_parts: Power-law loss scaling in parameters, tokens, or training compute.
Prediction of much larger runs from power laws fitted on smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and its trend with compute.
The study varies loop placement, number of looped layers, and maximum loop count, not ordinary depth and width sweeps or a broad range of architectures.
Other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, and transfer scaling laws.
Downstream predictability from parameter/token/pretraining-compute scale or pretraining loss; the reported downstream results vary inference loop count.
Fitted scaling exponents, compute-optimal splits, and dependence of those fits on fitting choices or curve bending.
